title: Xiaomi's Three Chips: Trading Resources for Time, Betting on a Paradigm Shift in On-Device AI
dek: Xiaomi unveiled three Xuanjie chips in one go, aggressively betting on memory interconnect, 3D stacking, and an all-AI architecture. It's trading resources for time, betting on a paradigm shift in on-device AI and vertical integration—but it still trails top-tier chip companies by a clear margin.
why: This episode offers an in-depth analysis of the technical choices and strategic logic behind Xiaomi's three chips. It's dense with information, with clear analogies for key technologies like memory interconnect and 3D stacking. Worth a listen for chip industry professionals and investors tracking Xiaomi.
who: Investors focused on Xiaomi's chip efforts, chip industry engineers, product managers, and tech professionals wanting to understand the on-device AI trend.
skip: The first 3 minutes, discussing the definition of self-developed chips, can be skipped—jump straight to the technical analysis.

points.h: Chip capability is about system definition, not IP self-reliance
points.body: To judge whether a company can make chips, don't just count how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; look at how much system definition power it holds. Xiaomi's Xuanjie O1 uses ARM IP for CPU and GPU, but system integration and physical implementation are its own. Apple and Qualcomm excel at iterating yearly and continuously taping out—something latecomers lack. Xiaomi doesn't have a decade to learn slowly, so it's taking an aggressive route, advancing multiple high-risk technology lines simultaneously.

points.h: O1's poor energy efficiency stems from a missing shared water tank
points.body: The Xuanjie O1 lacks a system-level cache (SLC), causing power consumption to spike under heavy GPU load and hurting energy efficiency. An SLC is like a shared water tank in a residential complex: the closer data is to the compute units, the faster the access and the lower the power. The O1 has many GPU cores but limited DDR bandwidth, so many cores sit idle waiting for data—that's the bandwidth wall. The O3 adds a 16MB SLC, splits it into multiple cache blocks distributed across the chip, and designs an on-chip network scheduler to handle data consistency and access conflicts.

points.h: ARM's generic bus forces Xuanjie to build its own
points.body: ARM's off-the-shelf CHI+CMN solution is too generic, retaining compatibility and redundancy that can't be tailored to Xuanjie. So the O3 uses a self-developed X-Ring unified fabric that is CHI-compatible but defines its own interconnect protocol, with a custom high-speed network hub and memory controller. This reduces protocol conversion overhead and lets data decide cache placement and paths based on need. Xiaomi claims protocol conversion overhead drops by 75%, and static access latency is 82 nanoseconds—32% lower than the O1, even beating Apple's A19 Pro.

points.h: Compute bottleneck shifts from matrix multiply to vector operations
points.body: The O3 adds AI units to every subsystem—CPU, GPU, ISP, etc.—so computation happens where the data resides, reducing data movement. The NPU core count drops from 6 to 4, but Tensor compute rises to 200 Tops, because Xiaomi judges that the bottleneck for large models is shifting from matrix multiplication to vector operations like Softmax, quantization, and KV cache. The vector unit is about the same area as the Tensor unit, with 6.8 times the multiply-accumulate units of the O1, and it introduces an SMT-like architecture, similar to CUDA, to handle irregular parallel tasks.

points.h: Chips and models should be co-defined by the same company
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with MEMO to compress INT4 weights to 5 bits using a 5-value quantization method, with almost no accuracy loss, reducing memory bandwidth and capacity needs by 30%. The 3-billion-parameter MEMO model runs on the O3, with prefill performance up 40% and decode up 45%. This ability to co-define chips and models is the closed-loop advantage of vertical integration—no need to wait for others to define a model and then adapt a generic chip.

points.h: 3nm performance is eked out one standard cell at a time
points.body: The O3 uses the more mature N3P process, delivering 5% better performance at the same power and 5%-10% lower power at the same frequency. Xiaomi also did extensive process optimization: self-developed standard cells grew from 480 in the O1 to over 2,400, covering various chip blocks; it compressed the power-supply buffer channels so power and signals route from the middle of modules, boosting transistor density by 5%. The CPU went from 4 clusters to 3 clusters with 10 all-large cores, improving single-core performance by 31% and multi-core by 60%, surpassing the A19 Pro.

points.h: Near-memory computing pushes phone memory bandwidth to 1.22TB/s
points.body: The Xuanjie O100 uses wafer-level 3D stacking: one compute wafer and two memory wafers stacked vertically, connected via hybrid bonding, forming a near-memory computing architecture. It uses thousands of shorter, denser vertical interconnects to achieve high bandwidth with lower energy per bit shift—like an HBM for phones. Data: 28,762 data connections, 1.22TB/s bandwidth, far exceeding the tens of bits wide connection of a traditional SoC to LPDDR. The compute layer has 14 independent cores, each paired with a RISC-V processor for control.

points.h: CXMT's value lies not in speed grade but in co-definition
points.body: Xiaomi partnered with CXMT to debut LPDDR6, reducing dependence on Samsung and SK Hynix. Even if CXMT offers the entry-level 10.667Gbps speed, Xiaomi can compensate for peak rate gaps with wider channels, a larger SLC, and a self-developed memory controller. More importantly, the two companies co-validate and tune from the design stage, jointly defining a Chinese mobile memory subsystem solution. For CXMT, this proves its high-speed I/O and physical layer capabilities, earning it a seat at the next-generation mobile memory table.

points.h: Xiaomi is betting not on chips but on a time window
points.body: First, it bets on a paradigm shift in on-device computing: AI's weight in the SoC is rising, phones become AI interaction gateways, and Xiaomi wants to stand in the definer's position. Second, it bets that vertical integration becomes a core competency for device makers—generic chips can't meet the fragmented needs of the human-car-home ecosystem, so it must own its compute architecture. Third, it bets on an uncertain time window, trading resources for time to compress the catch-up cycle, preferring to bear engineering risk rather than wait for the window to close.

points.h: Xuanjie is closing faster, but none of the three thresholds are crossed
points.body: Top-tier SoC companies need three capabilities: self-developed CPU/GPU microarchitecture, self-developed 5G baseband, and continuous multi-generation tape-outs with tens of millions of shipments. Xuanjie currently meets none of these, still clearly behind the first tier—it's just closing faster. What truly reshapes the industry isn't a single stunning chip but the sustained iteration capability built by a group of companies. Xuanjie's larger significance is proving Xiaomi's chip efforts haven't stopped and that it's moving forward with Chinese chip industry partners.

terms.def: A cache shared by multiple compute units within a chip, like a shared water tank in a residential complex.
A wafer-level 3D stacking interconnect technology that uses direct copper-to-copper connections for high bandwidth and low power.
Placing memory and compute units close together to reduce data movement distance, improving bandwidth and energy efficiency.
A performance bottleneck where data movement capability limits performance, so adding more compute cores doesn't help.
A parallel processing architecture that can manage multiple tasks simultaneously to improve utilization of compute units.

quotes.text: To judge whether a company can really make chips, don't just stare at how many IP blocks it hand-crafts; you should look at how much system definition power it holds.
Xiaomi isn't slowly learning to make chips; it's trading resources for time, trying to build, within a limited time window, the complete capability station that a mature chip company needs.
As long as data is stored reasonably and distributed efficiently, the entire chip can benefit.
Once it succeeds, it won't have to wait for models defined by others, then adapt generic chips to them, and then figure out how to stuff them into a phone.
It would rather bear more engineering and R&D uncertainty than wait until the window truly closes and regret not having moved faster.
